lines.english: When the Argyn and Kyrgyz, intermingled,
Had settled along the river,
And Karakan had passed from this world,
It was as though a fire had gone out,
With not a soul left to stand against them,
lines.note: The unusual form ‘каяшаякка’ is read as resistance or opposition.

lines.english: To utter a word of defiance
The great multitude had no strength left,
Molto Khan of the Chinese
Unleashed havoc,
Those who offered resistance
lines.note: ‘Каяшаяк’ is read as opposition or resistance.

lines.english: He slaughtered without sparing one.
He imposed excessive tribute,
And anyone who spoke back
He drenched in red blood,
He spared not a slender thread of life.
lines.note: ‘Кылча жан’ evokes life as thin as a hair; the wording is retained as an image of utter slaughter.

lines.english: When he gathered his force,
lines.note: The implied subject appears to be Molto Khan; the phrase can also mean taking courage or acting with renewed resolve.

lines.english: Of the many Kyrgyz and Argyn,
The blood surged like water,
Remembering Karakan,
The great multitudes wept.
The Argyn and Kyrgyz mingled together
When they camped along the river valley,
When Karakhan passed from this world
And it was as though a fire had gone out,
Not a soul remained to resist,
To speak a word of defiance
The great host had no strength left,
Molto Khan of the Chinese
Began the slaughter,
And anyone who resisted
He relentlessly cut down.
He imposed an excessive tribute,
And anyone who answered back
He dyed in crimson blood,
He did not spare so much as a hair's breadth of life.
When he rose in fury,
The blood of the multitude of Kyrgyz and Argyn
Flowed like water,
And when Karakhan came to mind,
The gathered peoples wept.
The Argyn and Kyrgyz, mingled together,
when they camped along the river,
when Karakan departed this world
and it was as though a fire had gone out,
with not a soul left to resist,
lines.note: The unusual word 'каяшаякка' is read here as referring to resistance or opposition, in light of the following lines.

lines.english: to utter a word of defiance
the great mass of people had no strength left.
Molto Khan of the Chinese
unleashed havoc,
and those who offered resistance
lines.note: 'Каяшаяк бергенди' is understood as those who opposed him; the precise unusual expression is uncertain.

lines.english: he slaughtered without sparing a single one.
He imposed a heavier tribute,
and anyone who answered back
he dyed in red blood,
sparing not even the slightest life.
When he grew emboldened,
lines.note: The subject is implicit; this is read as continuing to describe Molto Khan.

lines.english: of the multitude of Kyrgyz and Argyn
the blood surged like water,
and, remembering Karakan,
the many people wept.
The Argyn and Kyrgyz intermingled
When they encamped along the river valley,
When Karakhan passed from this world
And it was as though a fire had gone out,
Not a soul remained to resist,
lines.note: The source form "Каяшаякка" is unusual; it is read from context as referring to resistance or opposition.

lines.english: And to utter a word of protest
The great host of people had no strength left.
Molto Khan of the Chinese
Began the turmoil;
lines.note: "Калайман" can denote turmoil, havoc, or a violent mêlée; "turmoil" preserves the broad sense.

lines.english: Those who offered resistance
He slaughtered without sparing.
He assessed his tribute excessively;
Anyone who spoke back
He dyed in crimson blood,
Sparing not a single living soul.
When he rose in fury,
The blood of the multitude of Kyrgyz and Argyn
Surged like water;
Remembering Karakhan,
The multitudes wept.
Argyn and Kyrgyz together
when they had settled along the river,
when Karakhan had passed from this world
and it was as though a fire had gone out,
with not a soul left for kayashayak,
lines.note: The term kayashayak is unclear in context and is retained transliterated.

lines.english: to say kayasha
lines.note: The word kayasha is unclear in context and is retained transliterated.

lines.english: not one man of the great multitude remaining,
Moltо Khan of the Chinese
began the tumult,
those who gave kayashayak
lines.note: Kayashayak is unclear in context and is retained transliterated.

lines.english: he slaughtered without stopping.
He displayed a might beyond measure;
whoever spoke back
he stained with red blood,
leaving not even a shred of life.
When he had grown fierce,
of the numerous Kyrgyz and Argyn
the blood flowed like water;
Karakhan came to mind,
and the great multitudes wept.
Argyn and Kyrgyz, intermingled,
when they had camped along the river,
when Karakan passed from this world
and it was as though a fire had gone out,
not a soul was left to resist,
to utter words of defiance;
of the great multitude, none was left.
Molto Khan of the Chinese
began the slaughter.
Those who offered resistance
he slaughtered relentlessly.
He judged his strength to be greater;
whoever spoke back
he dyed in crimson blood.
He spared not a thread of life.
When he had grown emboldened,
of the many Kyrgyz and Argyn
the blood flowed like water.
Karakan came to mind,
and the many peoples wept.
Akbaltay gave his blessing,
In the marshes of the wide Altai,
lines.note: The form ‘баткалда’ is uncertain; read here as referring to marshy or muddy ground.

lines.english: While the Kyrgyz lay there grieving,
Days dragged on and nights passed,
Summer passed and autumn reached its midpoint,
It was the season when livestock grew fat;
Three months had elapsed.
The elder wife named Chyyyrdy,
She was Jakyp's wife—
Was pregnant and had developed cravings.
He slaughtered eighty mares from the horse herd,
Yet she was not satisfied with that meat,
That elder wife Chyyyrdy
Did not stop craving at all.
A set of nine animals, headed by a camel,
Jakyp slaughtered yet again,
Before his elder wife
He also laid the meat he had slaughtered.
Akbaltai gave his blessing.
In the marshes of vast Altai,
when the grieving Kyrgyz were dwelling there,
the day delayed and the night passed,
autumn reached its middle and summer passed,
the season of plenty
had come to fill three months' time.
The old woman named Chyyrdy,
the wife of Jakyp,
had developed strange cravings.
He slaughtered eighty mares from the herd,
yet she did not have her fill, saying, 'It is meat.'
that old woman Chyyrdy
did not give up her cravings at all.
A set of nine led by a camel,
and then Jakyp slaughtered livestock,
before the old woman
he set the meat he had slaughtered as well.
Akbaltai gave his blessing,
In the marshy ground of vast Altai,
lines.note: The form ‘баткалда’ is uncertain; it is read here as referring to muddy or marshy ground.

lines.english: While the Kyrgyz lay grieving,
Days wore on and nights passed,
Summer passed and autumn reached its middle,
It was the season when livestock were fat,
Three months had elapsed.
The matron named Chyiyrdy—
She was Jakyp's wife—
Was pregnant and had cravings.
He slaughtered eighty mares from the horse herd,
Meat though it was, she did not eat her fill,
That matron Chyiyrdy
Did not lose her cravings at all.
A set of nine animals, headed by a camel,
Jakyp slaughtered once more,
Before the matron
He also laid the meat he had slaughtered.
Akbaltay gave his blessing,
In the marshlands of the broad Altai,
When the Kyrgyz lay there grieving,
Days passed and nights went by,
Autumn reached its middle and summer passed,
It was the season of abundance,
And three months had run their course.
The matron named Chyyyrdy,
That wife of Jakyp,
Began to have the cravings of pregnancy.
lines.note: The wording literally suggests an uncertain or suspected pregnancy accompanied by cravings.

lines.english: He slaughtered eighty mares from the herd,
But she did not satisfy herself with their meat;
That matron Chyyyrdy
Did not give up her craving at all.
One group of nine, headed by a camel,
lines.note: A traditional livestock-counting expression; the nine animals are grouped under a camel.

lines.english: Jakyp slaughtered more livestock,
And before the matron
He laid the meat he had slaughtered.
Akbaltai gave his blessing,
while in the marshes of broad Altai
the Kyrgyz lay in sorrow.
The days lagged on and the nights passed,
autumn reached its middle and summer had gone by;
the season of plenty
had run its course for three months.
The senior wife named Chyyrdy,
the wife of Jakyp,
had developed a strange craving.
He slaughtered eighty mares from his horses,
but she was not satisfied with meat,
that senior wife, Chyyrdy,
and did not abandon her craving at all.
A set of nine, led by a camel,
and Jakyp slaughtered more livestock;
before the senior wife
he also set the meat he had slaughtered.
Akbaltai gave his blessing
in the marshlands of the broad Altai,
lines.note: The locative phrase continues into the next line.

lines.english: when the Kyrgyz lay there grieving.
Days grew late and nights passed;
summer passed and mid-autumn came.
The season of fattened abundance
had run its course for three months.
The matron named Chyiyrdy,
that wife of Jakyp,
became pregnant and suffered cravings.
lines.note: The phrase combines pregnancy with the cravings associated with it.

lines.english: He slaughtered eighty mares from the herd;
though it was meat, she was not satisfied.
That matron Chyiyrdy
did not lose her craving at all.
A set of nine livestock headed by a camel
lines.note: Bir toguz denotes a customary group of nine animals or valuables; here it is explicitly headed by a camel.

lines.english: Jakyp slaughtered as well,
and before the matron
he laid the slaughtered meat.
His thoughts turned elsewhere,
Rich Jakyp gave to Oshpur
The boy named Chong Jindi.
lines.note: Chong Jindi is retained as a proper name; literally, it can mean ‘Big Madman.’

lines.english: Chyiyrdy cried and wailed aloud,
Looping her sash around her neck,
Pleading as she called out to Oshpur:
‘My dear Oshpur Bai,
You were a giant dwelling in the river valley,
You were the keeper of Bai Jakyp’s many sheep.
We have abundant wealth, but no child;
This child, whom we received when we were as good as dead—
lines.note: The compact phrase literally says ‘this child seen when dying’ and refers to a child obtained very late or against hope.

lines.english: There is no way to curb his mischief.
I have made a silk coat; have him put it on.
Among the horses, Toruchaar—
Catch that swift steed and mount him on it.
Fasten the Kalmyk’s stone upon the crown of his head.
lines.note: The literal image is clear, but the precise identity or ritual purpose of the ‘Kalmyk’s stone’ is uncertain.

lines.english: I entrust him into your hands;
Raise him for another four years!’
After Oshpur took the boy,
And Bai Jakyp remained there,
He mounted him on Toruchaar,
And dressed him in the ashes of silk,
lines.note: The source literally reads ‘the ashes of silk’; the expression is obscure, so the unusual image is preserved.

lines.english: Trusting to providence, toward the sheep
Brave Oshpur took him along.
When Manas went to Oshpur,
He was not yet Manas then;
The hero had not yet come to bear the name Manas.
He turned his thoughts to something else,
Wealthy Jakyp entrusted to Oshpur
The boy named Chong Jindi—Great Madcap.
Chyiyrdy wept and wailed,
Draping her belt around her neck,
Pleading, calling out, ‘Oshpur bai!’:
‘My dear Oshpur bai,
You were a giant dwelling in the valley,
You had charge of wealthy Jakyp’s many sheep.
We have great wealth, but no child;
This child we had when we were all but dead—
lines.note: The phrase literally says ‘seen when dead’; it appears to express how late or desperately awaited the child was.

lines.english: There is no way to curb his mischief.
I have made a silk coat; have him wear it.
Among the horses is Toruchaar;
Catch that noble steed and have him ride it.
Be sure to fasten a Kalmyk stone to the crown of his head.
lines.note: The nature of the ‘Kalmyk stone’ is unclear; the unusual image is retained literally.

lines.english: I have placed him in your hands as a sacred trust;
Care for him for another four years!’
Once Oshpur had taken the boy,
Once wealthy Jakyp had stayed behind there,
He set him on Toruchaar,
Clothed him in the ashes of silk,
lines.note: ‘Ashes of silk’ renders the wording literally; this may be an idiomatic description of a silk garment, but its precise sense is uncertain.

lines.english: And, trusting to fate, toward the sheep
Brave Oshpur led him away.
When Manas went to Oshpur,
He had not yet become Manas,
Your champion had not yet gained the name Manas.
He turned his thoughts elsewhere,
and wealthy Jakyp gave to Oshpur
the boy called Chong Jindi.
Chyiyr wept and wailed,
with a cord around her neck,
pleading to Oshpurbai:
‘Dear wealthy Oshpur,
you were a giant lying in the valley,
you were master of wealthy Jakyp’s many sheep.
We have much wealth, but no child;
this child we had in old age—
there is no way to curb his wildness.
Dress him in a silk coat,
among the horses, catch Toruchaar,
the racehorse, and set him on it to ride,
and fasten a Kalmyk stone upon his crown.
lines.note: The exact sense of the ‘Kalmyk stone’ and the action requested is uncertain.

lines.english: I leave him in your care;
look after him for another four years!’
After Oshpur had taken the child,
and wealthy Jakyp had stayed behind,
he set him on Toruchaar,
and dressed him in silk’s ashes,
lines.note: The phrase is rendered literally; its idiomatic sense is uncertain.

lines.english: and, trusting to fate, toward the sheep
valiant Oshpur led him away.
When Manas came to Oshpur,
then he was not yet Manas,
the hero had not yet taken the name Manas.
He turned his thoughts to something else,
Wealthy Jakyp entrusted to Oshpur
The boy who bore the name Chong Jindi.
lines.note: The name means ‘Big Madman.’

lines.english: Chyiyrdy wept and cried aloud,
Putting her belt around her neck,
Pleading, calling out to Oshpur Bai:
‘My dear Oshpur Bai,
You were a giant lying in the valley,
You were in charge of wealthy Jakyp’s many sheep.
We have abundant wealth, but no children;
This child we had when we were all but dead—
lines.note: The phrase literally says ‘seen when dead,’ apparently emphasizing how late or desperately the child was obtained.

lines.english: There is no way to curb his wildness.
I have made a silk coat; have him wear it,
Among the horses is Toruchaar;
Catch that splendid steed and have him ride it,
Be sure to fasten the Kalmyk stone to the crown of his head.
lines.note: The identity and purpose of the ‘Kalmyk stone’ are unclear.

lines.english: I have placed him in your hands as a sacred trust;
Care for him for another four years!’
Once Oshpur had taken the boy,
Once wealthy Jakyp had stayed behind there,
He put him on Toruchaar,
Clothed him in the ashes of silk,
lines.note: ‘The ashes of silk’ is the literal reading of ‘торконун күлүн’; the intended fabric or expression is uncertain.

lines.english: And, taking his chances, toward the sheep
Brave Oshpur led him away.
When Manas went to Oshpur,
He had not yet become Manas,
Your hero had not yet come to bear the name Manas.
He turned his thoughts elsewhere,
Rich Jakyp gave to Oshpur
The boy named Chong Jindi.
lines.note: Chong Jindi literally means ‘Big Madman’ and is retained as a name.

lines.english: Chyiyrdy wept and cried out,
Looping her belt around her neck,
Begging and calling, ‘Oshpur bai!’
‘My dear Oshpur bai,
lines.note: The address literally invokes taking the speaker’s suffering upon oneself.

lines.english: You were a giant dwelling in the valley,
You were master of Bai Jakyp’s many sheep.
We have plenty of wealth, but no child;
This is the child we saw when we were as good as dead—
lines.note: The phrase is literally ‘the child seen when dying’ and likely refers to a long-awaited child born late in life.

lines.english: There is no way to curb his mischief.
I have made a silk coat; have him put it on.
Among the horses is Toruchaar—
Catch that swift steed and mount him on it.
See that you fasten the Kalmak’s stone upon the crown of his head.
lines.note: The precise nature of ‘the Kalmak’s stone’ is unclear; the unusual image is translated literally.

lines.english: I place him in your hands as a sacred trust;
Raise him for another four years!’
After Oshpur took the boy,
After Bai Jakyp remained there,
He mounted him on Toruchaar,
And dressed him in the bloom of silk,
lines.note: The source literally has ‘the ash/bloom of silk’; ‘bloom’ is a tentative contextual reading.

lines.english: And, trusting to fate, toward the sheep
Brave Oshpur took him along.
When Manas went to Oshpur,
He had not yet become Manas then,
Your valiant one had not yet taken the name Manas.
He turned his thoughts elsewhere,
and wealthy Jakyp gave Oshpur
the boy named Chon Jindi.
Chyiyr wept and cried out,
with a rope put around her neck,
pleading, calling out to Oshpur:
‘Dear Oshpur the wealthy,
you were like a giant lying in the valley,
the master of wealthy Jakyp’s many sheep.
We have abundant possessions, but no child;
this child we had in our old age—
there is no way to restrain his wildness.
I made him a brocade coat; have him wear it.
Among the horses, Toruchaar,
catch that racing steed and let him ride it.
Put a Kalmyk stone on top of his head,
lines.note: The exact significance of the ‘Kalmyk stone’ is uncertain.

lines.english: I entrust him to your hands;
care for him another four years!’
After Oshpur took the boy,
after wealthy Jakyp remained there,
he put Toruchaar under him to ride,
and dressed him in Torqo’s ash-gray garment,
lines.note: The phrase rendered ‘Torqo’s ash-gray garment’ is idiomatic/uncertain.

lines.english: and, taking a chance, toward the sheep
brave Oshpur led him about.
When Manas went to Oshpur,
he had not yet become Manas,
your valiant Manas had not yet mounted a horse.
Kochku came swaggering,
lines.note: The expressive word ‘короктоп’ is read as describing a swaggering manner; its precise nuance is uncertain.

lines.english: His champions looming tall,
Mounted on a red-chestnut horse,
Having ridden out in fury,
Having received a letter from Esenkan.
What could poor Kochku do?
From the skilled sentries,
lines.note: The syntax is compressed; this is read with the following lines as specifying the men selected for his force.

lines.english: From the best at thrusting spears,
Taking a force of some seven hundred,
That Kochku had come,
His short coat bulging out,
lines.note: ‘Күрмөчө’ is read as a short coat or jacket; the exact garment and the expressive verb are uncertain.

lines.english: His mail coat spreading broad.
Dust flew into the sky,
The army marched in a pounding throng.
What the soldiers bore slung on them
Were mighty bows and lacquered arrows.
lines.note: ‘Алеңгир’ is provisionally read as an epithet meaning mighty; ‘сыр жебе’ as lacquered or painted arrows.

lines.english: Upon wealthy Jakyp's head
He brought trouble.
lines.note: ‘Аңгеме’ literally denotes talk or a story; here it is read idiomatically as trouble or a disturbing affair.

lines.english: His roaring split stone,
Kochku came gathering fury,
His shouting split heads:
Kochku came in a menacing rush,
His champions in groups of forty,
lines.note: The form сороктоп most likely means grouped or counted by forties.

lines.english: Riding a red bay horse,
Setting out in fury,
Having received a letter from Esen Khan—
What else could poor Kochku do?
From the ablest of the sentries,
From the mightiest spear-thrusters,
Taking a force of some seven hundred,
That Kochku had indeed come,
Making his short coat bulge,
Making his mail coat spread wide.
lines.note: Бадана denotes mail armor; the precise motion conveyed by барбайтып is uncertain.

lines.english: Dust flew up to the sky,
The army advanced in a cloud of dust.
What the soldiers had slung on themselves
Were alengir bows and painted arrows.
lines.note: Алеңгир is retained as a transliterated descriptor for a type or quality of bow whose exact sense is uncertain.

lines.english: Upon Bai Jakyp's head
The affair came crashing down.
His bellow split stone,
Kochku came surging with fury,
His shout splitting heads:
Kochku came swaggering,
lines.note: The expressive word ‘короктоп’ is read as swaggering; its precise shade of movement is uncertain.

lines.english: His champions looming tall,
Riding a red-chestnut horse,
Setting out in fury,
Bearing a letter from Esenkan,
What could poor Kochku do?
From among the skilled sentries,
From among the stout spear-thrusters,
Taking a force of some seven hundred,
That Kochku had come,
His short coat bulging,
lines.note: The garment term ‘күрмөчө’ and the expressive description are read as a short coat bulging out.

lines.english: His coat of mail spreading broad,
Dust flying to the sky,
The army marching in a rumbling throng,
What the soldiers bore slung upon them:
Mighty bows and lacquered arrows.
lines.note: ‘Алеңгир’ is provisionally read as an epithet meaning mighty; the exact kind or quality of bow is uncertain.

lines.english: Upon wealthy Jakyp's head
He brought trouble.
lines.note: ‘Аңгеме,’ literally a story or matter, is read here as trouble brought upon Jakyp.

lines.english: His bellow splitting stone,
Kochku came gathering force,
His shouts splitting heads:
Kochku came in a show of strength,
with his champions in scores of forty,
mounted on red-dun horses,
setting out in anger,
having received a letter from Esen Khan.
What was poor Kochku to do?
Taking men from among the skilled guards,
the experts at thrusting spears,
he took a force of about seven hundred;
thus had that Kochku come,
making his outer garment flutter,
making his coat of mail gleam,
with dust flying up to the sky,
as the army marched, raising dust.
What the soldiers bore
were great bows and secret arrows.
To Bay Jakyp's ears
the news was brought.
His bellowing split the stones;
Kochku came worked up,
his shouting splitting heads:
Kökchü came, splendidly arrayed,
his champions in groups of forty,
mounted on red-bay horses,
he set out in anger,
having received a letter from Esen Khan;
what else could poor Kökchü do?
taking skilled sentries,
men adept at thrusting spears,
and a force of some seven hundred,
that Kökchü had come.
Making his short coat flap,
making his coat of mail swell out,
dust flew up to the sky;
the army marched, kicking up dust.
What the soldiers bore
were curved bows and hidden arrows;
to Bay Jakyp's ears
the report came.
His bellowing split the rocks,
Kökchü came in full battle-fury,
his cry splitting heads:
Kochku came, roaring threats,
lines.note: The adverb 'koroktop' can imply making a fearsome or threatening display.

lines.english: His champions drawn up in ranks,
lines.note: The precise nuance of 'soroktop' is uncertain; it appears to describe the champions being marshalled or arrayed.

lines.english: Mounted on a chestnut horse,
lines.note: Literally, a 'red bay/chestnut' horse.

lines.english: He set out in fury,
Having received a letter from Esenkhan,
What else could poor Kochku do?
Taking men fit to stand guard,
lines.note: The syntax continues through the following lines; 'yktuu' conveys capable, dependable, or formidable men.

lines.english: Strong men who could thrust a spear,
Taking an army of some seven hundred,
That Kochku had come.
lines.note: This line completes the report begun in the preceding lines.

lines.english: Making his short coat billow,
lines.note: The verb suggests the garment puffing or flaring out.

lines.english: Making his mail armor gleam,
lines.note: The exact verb is uncertain, but the line appears to describe the visual display of his mail armor.

lines.english: Dust flew up to the sky,
As the army marched, raising clouds of dust,
What the soldiers had slung upon them
lines.note: This line continues into the next line.

lines.english: Were alengir bows and polished arrows.
lines.note: 'Alengir' is an uncertain traditional descriptor for the bow; 'syr' may mean ornamented, polished, or coated.

lines.english: Upon rich Jakyp's head
lines.note: This line continues into the next line.

lines.english: The affair came crashing down.
lines.note: Literally, the tale or affair reached/fell upon Jakyp's head, meaning the danger or trouble arrived.

lines.english: His bellowing split the stones,
Kochku came surging with fury,
His battle cry split heads.
